summary: Deep technical workshop to design and validate Helios Financial's private VPC deployment for Redwood inference. Focus on NAT/egress reliability (soak testing), KV cache behavior across AZs, batching tradeoffs for latency vs throughput, and quantization plans. Agreed next steps include NAT soak window, sharing runbooks and scripts, and a short benchmark plan with target p95 latency and KV cache hit goals.
topics: hairpinning and MTU impact on latency
KV cache eviction and cross-AZ consistency
continuous batching config and max latency SLOs
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-12-08 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 72 minutes
- Recording: yes (fireflies export)

[00:00] Samira (AE): all right hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna get started. i'm samira from redwood, with jonah on platform and elena from infra. thanks for making time.
[00:12] Marcus (Infra): thanks, yeah appreciate it. we wanted to do a focused session on the private vpc egress cause we're seeing weird p95 spikes during load tests.
[00:22] Jonah (SE): cool, quick agenda — NAT soak planning, kv-cache behavior under partial misses, batching knobs and latency targets, and quantization fallback testing. sound good?
[00:30] Priya (ML): yep, that's perfect. our goals are basically p95 under 220ms for 512 token context, and steady throughput for concurrent sessions.
[00:40] Daniel (Security): i'll caveat we need full audit logs and KMS integration for keys — also SOC2 audit is upcoming so anything that impacts cross-account endpoints we need to document.

[02:05] Jonah: quick technical background — in private VPC mode Redwood creates interface endpoints and, depending on customer choice, egress can go through a NAT gateway or via PrivateLink. NAT introduces hairpinning for intra-VPC calls if your egress is to the same AZ, and that can impact MTU and path MTU discovery.
[02:40] Marcus: when you say hairpin, do you mean source/dest get rewritten so packets leave and come back to same host? we've seen packet fragmentation which seems to increase RTT.
[02:51] Elena: yes exactly; if your route table sends outbound through a centralized NAT, the packets may go out and back — and if MTU isn't consistent across the path you'll see fragmentation. We've got mixed MTUs because some on-prem links are 9000 and cloud is 1500.

[05:10] Jonah: two quick mitigations — enable path MTU discovery and enforce 1500 across the egress path, or prefer regional PrivateLink so traffic never hits the NAT. PrivateLink avoids hairpin but requires cross-account endpoint policies and DNS override.
[05:38] Marcus: PrivateLink sounds ideal but our security team wants to avoid cross-account peering; is PrivateLink still okay with strong policies?
[05:46] Daniel: we can accept PrivateLink if we can show endpoint policies + VPC endpoint service with explicit principals, plus audit logs. also need SNI and mTLS for the endpoint.

[08:20] Jonah: noted. On KV cache — Redwood's runtime keeps the per-session KV cache on the worker; cache hits avoid re-computing key/value states which is big for long contexts. But when we scale across AZs we see cache misses if sticky routing to the same worker isn't enforced.
[08:45] Priya: our traffic pattern includes a lot of short-lived sessions that later get resumed from different front-ends. KV hit rate drops from ~85% to 40% during spikes.
[09:01] Jonah: yep, that explains the p95 jump — a cold KV miss is effectively rewarming which costs ~30–120ms depending on model and GPU. We recommend session affinity (consistent hashing) at the router level or a shared in-memory KV (but that has sharding/consistency costs).

[11:12] Tara (SRE): what's the operational plan if we enforce affinity? does that reduce our ability to autoscale?
[11:18] Elena: it can, slightly — affinity increases load skew, but we can combine with local warmers that prepopulate KV for predicted sessions. Also autoscaling policies can be per-pool with min replicas per-AZ to avoid thundering rebalances.

[14:00] Marcus: ok pragmatic question — for our initial pilot should we do NAT egress with MTU normalization or go full PrivateLink? which path gets us to the p95 goal faster?
[14:16] Jonah: fastest is NAT with a controlled soak window — normalize MTU, ensure ELB/IGW settings, and run a 48-hour soak to surface intermittent hairpin issues. PrivateLink adds configuration time but reduces network variance. So pilot: NAT soak first, then PrivateLink if we hit edge cases.

[16:55] Priya: hopping to batching — we saw that increasing batch size to 8 improved throughput but p95 jumped. what's the recommended continuous batching config?
[17:05] Jonah: continuous batching trades off latency for throughput. Key knobs: max_batch_size, max_batch_wait_ms, and priority routing for low-latency callers. For p95 < 220ms we suggest max_batch_size=4 and max_batch_wait_ms=30ms as a starting point for your model on H100. For batch sizes higher than 4 we edge into slower p95s.
[17:40] Samira: note that kernel selection also matters — quantized kernels have different per-token latency. If you use 4-bit quant and fallback to int8 for certain ops, you'll see variability.

[19:20] Priya: about quantization — we plan to try 4-bit for model-X to save cost. what are the priority regressions we should watch?
[19:30] Jonah: watch instruction-level output diffs, tokenization edge cases, and failure fallback latency. Mechanically, 4-bit (q4) reduces memory but sometimes triggers slower kernels on certain operators; measure p50/p95 and check token-level perplexity on a validation prompt set. We'll provide a quant profile that pins per-layer fallback to higher precision if a layer is unstable.

[22:00] Marcus: any guidance on running the quant bench inside private VPC? we want to avoid sending eval data out of Helios.
[22:10] Elena: you can run the quant bench in your VPC with our private agent image; Redwood provides an OCI image that runs locally and uploads only aggregated results. We'll share the runbook and the image tag.

[24:30] Jonah: back to NAT soak — the soak should include: synthetic steady-state traffic, peak ramp tests, and session-resume patterns. Key metrics: p50/p95 latency, KV hit rate, TCP retransmits, and MTU path changes.
[24:45] Tara: for observability we need token-level tracing and per-token timings — can Redwood provide a way to annotate traces with model version and quant profile?
[24:56] Jonah: yes — the runtime emits per-token timing and model/variant tags; in private mode we can forward those to your Datadog/CloudWatch via a VPC L2 forwarder. We'll include sample dashboards.

[27:10] Marcus: earlier you said cold KV miss cost ~30–120ms. can you quantify for our expected model (Model-X on A100 w/ 512 context)?
[27:20] Jonah: approximate numbers: warm token generation ~8–12ms/token p50 on A100, kv-rewarm penalty ~80–110ms depending on whether it's a blocked operator or memory copy across GPU. H100 will be a bit lower. We should run a quick baseline in your env to get precise numbers.

[30:05] Priya: on cross-AZ routing — if we pin sessions to an AZ but then that AZ loses a node, how fast is failover and what's the cold-start exposure?
[30:14] Elena: failover depends on health checks. Our default is 30s deregistration then new session gets routed — which can cause cold KV misses. We recommend healthcheck tuning and a small standby pool per-AZ to reduce cold starts.

[33:50] Jonah: quick demo, sorry brief screen-share glitch earlier — showing KV hit ratio graphs, p95 spikes correlating with retransmit bursts, and a sample batching config that kept p95 within target with max_batch_wait_ms=25ms and max_batch_size=4.

[40:00] Marcus: question for security — SSO and KMS — can we use our HSM provider and have Redwood integrate with customer-managed KMS?
[40:12] Daniel: we need to ensure key usage never leaves our control.
[40:18] Elena: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS and HSM in private deployments; keys can be mounted via KMS plugin and audit logs include envelope metadata. We'll attach the integration doc.

[42:45] Priya: about the quant profile — will the runtime auto-fallback if the int4 operator regresses? how transparent is that?
[42:55] Jonah: yes, the runtime has a policy: if an operator exceeds a configured error threshold on the validation shard, it falls back to int8 for that operator and logs the event. This adds a few ms for the first fallback event; subsequent runs are pinned.

[46:30] Tara: one operational concern — NAT gateway scaling and ephemeral ports. during our load test we saw TCP port exhaustion occasionally. suggestions?
[46:40] Jonah: recommend NAT gateway autoscaling added with multiple NAT instances per AZ and source port mapping to reduce exhaustion. Alternatively, egress proxy with connection pooling (squid-like) reduces ephemeral port usage but introduces a hop. For low-latency calls, avoid additional proxy hops unless necessary.

[50:00] Marcus: if we move to PrivateLink, what's the latency delta we should expect vs NAT?
[50:10] Jonah: PrivateLink typically removes 10–40ms of variance from p95 in our experience for similar workloads because traffic doesn't traverse IGW/NAT. Exact delta depends on topology.

[52:30] Priya: can we run a 24–48 hour A/B: NAT vs PrivateLink during the pilot? we'd like side-by-side metrics.
[52:38] Samira: yes — we can help run parallel tests if you can provide subnet and route table changes. We'll help script the traffic generator and consolidate metrics.

[55:20] Jonah: final engineering checklist we recommend for the pilot:
- enforce MTU 1500 on egress path OR configure jumbo frames consistently
- spin up NAT soak with multiple NAT IPs per AZ for 48 hours
- enable session affinity at the router or consistent hashing
- instrument KV hit metrics and per-token timing
- start with continuous batching params (max_batch_size=4, max_wait_ms=30)
- apply conservative quant profile, run local bench image, validate token diffs

[58:01] Marcus: sounds good. some quick open questions from our side — how do you recommend we measure token-level regressions and who owns rollback?
[58:14] Jonah: we recommend a token-diff harness sending your validation prompt set and calculating percent token-level delta and perplexity; rollback controlled by your ops team but Redwood can provide automatic rollout gates (canary + rollback on metric regression).

[60:45] Priya: any quick gotchas for on-prem links? we've got MPLS segments with varying MTU and sometimes deep packet inspection boxes.
[60:55] Elena: DPI boxes often break path MTU discovery; we suggest bypassing DPI for inference egress or negotiate consistent MTU. Also watch for TLS interception or SNI rewrite which breaks mTLS to endpoints.

[64:00] Samira: wrapping up — recap of next steps: Jonah will share scripts and dashboards, elena will send runbook and agent image tag, marcus to confirm soak window and subnet IDs, priya to provide prompt set and perf target.
[64:20] Daniel: we'll also want a security appendix for the SOC2 folks.

[66:30] Samira: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up in writing and post the runbook in the shared drive. meeting adjourned.
